Verify Now Blog > Reflow Soldering vs. Wave Soldering: Key Differences and PCB Design Tips Reflow Soldering vs. Wave Soldering: Key Differences and PCB Design Tips by: Mila Oct 16,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout Reflow Soldering Wave Soldering SMT vs. THT PCB Assembly PCB Soldering As hardware engineers, we design the PCB, select the components, and send the Gerber files to the manufacturer. But have you ever wondered why some components go through reflow soldering while others require wave soldering? Both processes melt solder to form electrical and mechanical connections, so why does a production line need two different types of equipment? The reason is not that equipment manufacturers are making the process unnecessarily complicated. The main difference between reflow soldering and wave soldering lies in how the solder reaches the joints and which types of components each process is best suited for. For hardware engineers, understanding these two processes is more than just useful knowledge. It can affect PCB layout , component selection, pad design, and even troubleshooting during manufacturing. How Reflow Soldering Works Reflow soldering is primarily used for surface-mount technology (SMT) components, such as resistors, capacitors, SOPs, QFNs, and BGAs. The basic process is straightforward: solder paste is first printed onto the PCB pads, and the components are then placed on the board. Next, the PCB assembly passes through a reflow oven, where the solder paste goes through several stages, including preheating, heating, time above the liquidus temperature, and cooling. These stages allow the solder to melt, wet the surfaces, and solidify to form reliable joints. One detail that is easy to overlook is that reflow soldering is not simply about heating the entire PCB to a fixed temperature. The temperature profile over time must be carefully controlled. Taking the common SAC305 lead-free solder alloy as an example, its melting range is approximately 217–220°C. During reflow, the solder joint temperature must rise above the liquidus temperature and remain there for a certain period. However, the peak temperature, time above liquidus, and heating and cooling rates depend on factors such as the solder paste, component temperature limits, and PCB thermal mass. These parameters cannot be applied universally to every board. （reflow soldering） How Wave Soldering Works Imagine a PCB with small resistors, large connectors, and power pads connected to extensive copper areas. Small components generally have lower thermal mass and heat up quickly, while large components and pads absorb more heat and may heat up more slowly. If the temperature rises too quickly, the small components may approach their peak temperature before the solder on the larger pads has fully melted. On the other hand, increasing the peak temperature too much or extending the time at high temperatures to accommodate the larger pads can increase thermal stress on components, damage the PCB, and raise the risk of solder oxidation. The equipment melts the solder and uses a pump to create a stable wave of molten solder. After the PCB passes through flux application and preheating, its solder side comes into contact with the molten solder. The solder wets the component leads and PCB pads, forming the joints. Traditional wave soldering is most commonly used for through-hole technology (THT) components, such as through-hole connectors, transformers, relay sockets, and some power components. Their leads pass through holes in the PCB, allowing the molten solder to contact the leads and pads from the solder side and form reliable joints. If the board contains a large number of surface-mount components, especially fine-pitch leads or packages with bottom-side pads, solder may bridge adjacent leads or cause soldering defects in components that are unsuitable for this process. However, this does not mean that surface-mount components can never be wave soldered. When wave soldering is used for suitable SMT components, the component orientation, pad spacing, and solder mask design must be considered carefully. In some cases, adhesive is also used to hold the components in place during soldering. PCB travel direction, protruding lead length, and component placement on the solder side must also be taken into account. If the design is unsuitable, even well-adjusted equipment parameters may not be enough to ensure consistent production quality. Other processes, including selective wave soldering and pin-in-paste soldering (also known as intrusive reflow soldering), are used in actual manufacturing. The appropriate method depends on package structures, component distribution, solder joint reliability, and production requirements. （PCB Assembly） PCB Design Considerations for Reflow and Wave Soldering 1. Component and Pad Design For SMT packages such as QFNs and BGAs, engineers need to consider pad dimensions, solder paste printing, stencil design, and the reflow temperature profile. Package and pad design affect not only electrical performance but also soldering quality during PCB assembly. 2. Copper Distribution and Thermal Management When a power component's pad is connected to a large copper area, the copper can absorb and distribute heat, making it more difficult for the local pad to reach the required temperature. This may prevent the solder from melting sufficiently. During design, engineers should evaluate copper distribution, pad structure, and the actual temperature profile rather than simply increasing the oven temperature to compensate. 3. When these defects occur, engineers should investigate the PCB design and soldering process alongside the components themselves. Hardware engineers do not necessarily need to operate soldering equipment themselves, but they should understand how their designs affect manufacturability. Reflow soldering focuses on controlling the temperature profile during solder paste melting, while wave soldering focuses on controlling the contact between molten solder and the PCB's solder side. Neither process is universally better than the other. The right choice depends on component packages, PCB layout, and production requirements. Why Do PCBs Need Stitching Vias Along the Board Edge? by: Mila Oct 07,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout stitching vias PCB EMI shielding PCB return path PCB via stitching Anyone who has worked on PCB layout has probably experienced this: after finishing the layout, you hand the board over to a senior engineer for review. They take a quick look around the board and ask, “Where are the ground vias along the edge?” At first, this may seem unnecessary. After all, the board edge does not carry signal traces. So why are stitching vias placed there? The answer lies in what happens around the edge of a PCB. Properly placed grounding vias can help control electromagnetic coupling, provide a more continuous high-frequency return path, and improve PCB edge shielding. For high-speed, RF, and EMI-sensitive designs, that simple row of vias can make a noticeable difference. （Stitching Vias） What Do Ground Vias Along the PCB Edge Actually Do? This row of vias is commonly known as a ground via fence, via fence, or stitching vias. It is not simply a matter of placing a row of vias around the board. Instead, the vias connect ground structures on different PCB layers and create a more continuous electromagnetic boundary along the board edge. For high-speed, RF, and high-reliability PCBs, the main benefits include improving high-frequency return paths, reducing electromagnetic leakage and coupling, and enhancing the continuity of local shielding structures. 1. Reduce Electromagnetic Leakage and Improve EMI Performance The PCB edge is the boundary between copper, dielectric material, and air. When high-speed, clock, or RF signals pass through the board, relatively strong electromagnetic fields may exist around this region. If the reference ground structure around the PCB edge is discontinuous, electromagnetic fields can couple outward through the edge, increasing EMI risks. External interference can also couple into sensitive circuits through the same region. A continuous row of grounding vias creates a low-impedance grounding boundary around the PCB edge. It can help limit the spread of electromagnetic fields around the edge and reduce coupling between the signals and the surrounding environment, improving EMI performance. 2. Provide a More Continuous High-Frequency Return Path High-speed signal return current generally follows a path close to the signal trace and its reference plane. When a PCB contains multiple ground or reference planes, insufficient connections between these planes can force high-frequency return currents to take longer paths, increasing both return path length and loop area. Stitching vias can provide low-impedance connections between different ground layers, giving high-frequency currents a more continuous return path. The more continuous the return path, the smaller the loop area can be, making electromagnetic radiation and crosstalk easier to control. 3. Help Reduce Edge Coupling and Local Resonance For RF, microwave, and high-speed clock PCBs, discontinuities around the board edge can create additional electromagnetic coupling paths and, at certain frequencies, may contribute to unwanted resonance. A continuous row of grounding vias can improve the electromagnetic boundary conditions around the PCB edge, reduce edge coupling, and help suppress local resonance. This is particularly useful in RF regions, shielding areas, and areas with dense high-speed signals, where a properly designed PCB ground via fence can be more effective than simply adding more copper. 4. Provide a Continuous Grounding Point for Shielding Cans RF modules and high-speed precision modules often use metal shielding cans. In this case, grounding vias can work together with the shielding-can solder pad to create a more continuous low-impedance grounding path around the shield. If a shielding can has only a few grounding points, the parasitic inductance of the connection path can affect high-frequency shielding performance. Adding stitching vias around the shielding-can edge can shorten the high-frequency current path and reduce electromagnetic leakage around the shield. Therefore, a via fence around a shielding can is generally more suitable for high-frequency shielding than a single-point ground connection. （EMI shielding + stitching vias） Faraday Cage: Why Can a Row of Ground Vias Help With Shielding? Many engineers think of the grounding vias around a PCB edge as a small Faraday cage. There is some truth to this analogy, but an important point should be noted: a PCB via fence is not an ideal, completely enclosed Faraday cage. The basic idea behind a Faraday cage is to use a continuous conductive structure to shield against electromagnetic fields through reflection, absorption, and boundary effects. On a PCB, continuous ground copper, reference planes, stitching vias, and metal shielding cans can work together to create a similar shielding structure. One important function of the grounding vias is to connect ground structures on different layers and reduce electromagnetic “openings” around the PCB edge. At high frequencies, shielding effectiveness depends on many factors, including conductor continuity, via spacing, opening size, material, operating frequency, and the overall structure. Therefore, instead of simply applying a fixed wavelength ratio, the via spacing should be determined based on the actual operating frequency, signal rise time, and PCB structure. For high-speed digital signals, the relevant frequency content is not necessarily equal to the clock frequency. Signal rise time also needs to be considered. Limitations A PCB via fence cannot completely prevent electromagnetic coupling at all frequencies. Copper and grounding vias alone have limited effectiveness against low-frequency magnetic fields. At high frequencies, the parasitic inductance, spacing, and structure of the vias can affect shielding performance. The effectiveness of the shielding structure also depends on the PCB reference planes, return paths, connectors, shielding cans, and other design elements. How Should You Design Stitching Vias Along the PCB Edge? Adding vias around the board is not simply a matter of placing them in a row. Via spacing, location, grounding method, and edge copper design all need to be considered according to the actual PCB structure. Here are some common design principles. 1. Via Spacing A common engineering approach is to estimate the via spacing based on the wavelength corresponding to the target frequency. For example, λ/10 or a smaller spacing can be used as an initial reference. However, this is not a fixed standard that applies to every PCB. Actual design should also consider: The highest frequency of interest High-speed signal rise/fall time PCB stackup Reference plane location Board-edge structure Shielding-can and connector openings For ordinary PCBs, relatively wider via spacing may be sufficient. For high-speed, RF, or high-EMI areas, the spacing may need to be reduced. Common engineering reference values include: General PCBs: approximately 50–100 mil High-speed/RF areas: approximately 30–50 mil Areas with stringent shielding requirements: further spacing reduction based on simulation or actual EMI testing Do not mechanically apply a fixed value. The final via spacing should be determined based on the actual frequency and structure. 2. Via Location Edge grounding vias should maintain an appropriate clearance from the PCB outline. Sufficient clearance should be provided according to the PCB manufacturer's fabrication capability to prevent damage to the vias during routing, milling, V-cut, or other board-edge processing. At the same time: Distribute the vias evenly along the board edge whenever possible. Avoid large gaps in the via fence. Increase via density around RF, high-speed signal, and connector areas when necessary. Connect the grounding vias to the appropriate reference ground plane rather than only to the top-layer copper. It is important to note that not every ground plane needs to be connected through the same via. The exact connection method should be determined based on the PCB stackup and return-current path. 3. Start With Continuous Ground Copper Many designers add a row of vias but overlook the ground copper between them. This alone cannot create a complete PCB ground via fence. A continuous ground copper area should be provided around the PCB edge according to the board structure, with grounding vias connecting it to the internal reference ground plane. The vias provide vertical connections, while continuous ground copper provides horizontal connections. Together, they form a more complete grounding boundary. High-speed signal traces, slots, or other structures should not arbitrarily cut through this grounding boundary. 4. Increase Via Density in Critical Areas The entire PCB does not necessarily need the same via spacing. The following areas may require additional stitching vias: Board-edge connectors and interfaces: Connectors are important paths through which external signals enter the PCB. Proper grounding vias can improve the return path around the interface and reduce edge coupling. Shielding-can areas: Dense grounding vias around the shielding-can solder pad can create a more continuous high-frequency grounding path. RF and high-speed clock areas: For areas that are particularly sensitive to EMI or crosstalk, reducing the via spacing can strengthen local shielding. Conclusion Proper stitching vias are an important part of high-speed PCB layout and PCB design .Their core function is to improve high-frequency return paths around the PCB edge and reduce electromagnetic coupling and EMI leakage through the combination of stitching vias and continuous reference-ground structures. For high-speed, RF, and EMI-sensitive PCBs, proper PCB via stitching and PCB edge shielding are particularly important. But remember: more vias are not always better, and not every PCB needs a dense row of grounding vias. Via spacing, edge clearance, reference planes, and local shielding structures should all be determined based on the actual signal frequency, rise time, and PCB stackup. It can help limit the spread of electromagnetic fields around the edge and reduce coupling between the signals and the surrounding environment, improving EMI performance. 2. Provide a More Continuous High-Frequency Return Path High-speed signal return current generally follows a path close to the signal trace and its reference plane. When a PCB contains multiple ground or reference planes, insufficient connections between these planes can force high-frequency return currents to take longer paths, increasing both return path length and loop area. Stitching vias can provide low-impedance connections between different ground layers, giving high-frequency currents a more continuous return path. The more continuous the return path, the smaller the loop area can be, making electromagnetic radiation and crosstalk easier to control. 3. Help Reduce Edge Coupling and Local Resonance For RF, microwave, and high-speed clock PCBs, discontinuities around the board edge can create additional electromagnetic coupling paths and, at certain frequencies, may contribute to unwanted resonance. A continuous row of grounding vias can improve the electromagnetic boundary conditions around the PCB edge, reduce edge coupling, and help suppress local resonance. This is particularly useful in RF regions, shielding areas, and areas with dense high-speed signals, where a properly designed PCB ground via fence can be more effective than simply adding more copper. 4. Provide a Continuous Grounding Point for Shielding Cans RF modules and high-speed precision modules often use metal shielding cans. In this case, grounding vias can work together with the shielding-can solder pad to create a more continuous low-impedance grounding path around the shield. If a shielding can has only a few grounding points, the parasitic inductance of the connection path can affect high-frequency shielding performance. Adding stitching vias around the shielding-can edge can shorten the high-frequency current path and reduce electromagnetic leakage around the shield. Therefore, a via fence around a shielding can is generally more suitable for high-frequency shielding than a single-point ground connection. （EMI shielding + stitching vias） Faraday Cage: Why Can a Row of Ground Vias Help With Shielding? Many engineers think of the grounding vias around a PCB edge as a small Faraday cage. There is some truth to this analogy, but an important point should be noted: a PCB via fence is not an ideal, completely enclosed Faraday cage. The basic idea behind a Faraday cage is to use a continuous conductive structure to shield against electromagnetic fields through reflection, absorption, and boundary effects. On a PCB, continuous ground copper, reference planes, stitching vias, and metal shielding cans can work together to create a similar shielding structure. One important function of the grounding vias is to connect ground structures on different layers and reduce electromagnetic “openings” around the PCB edge. At high frequencies, shielding effectiveness depends on many factors, including conductor continuity, via spacing, opening size, material, operating frequency, and the overall structure. Therefore, instead of simply applying a fixed wavelength ratio, the via spacing should be determined based on the actual operating frequency, signal rise time, and PCB structure. For high-speed digital signals, the relevant frequency content is not necessarily equal to the clock frequency. Signal rise time also needs to be considered. Limitations A PCB via fence cannot completely prevent electromagnetic coupling at all frequencies. Copper and grounding vias alone have limited effectiveness against low-frequency magnetic fields. At high frequencies, the parasitic inductance, spacing, and structure of the vias can affect shielding performance. The effectiveness of the shielding structure also depends on the PCB reference planes, return paths, connectors, shielding cans, and other design elements. How Should You Design Stitching Vias Along the PCB Edge? Adding vias around the board is not simply a matter of placing them in a row. Via spacing, location, grounding method, and edge copper design all need to be considered according to the actual PCB structure. Here are some common design principles. 1. Via Spacing A common engineering approach is to estimate the via spacing based on the wavelength corresponding to the target frequency. For example, λ/10 or a smaller spacing can be used as an initial reference. However, this is not a fixed standard that applies to every PCB. Actual design should also consider: The highest frequency of interest High-speed signal rise/fall time PCB stackup Reference plane location Board-edge structure Shielding-can and connector openings For ordinary PCBs, relatively wider via spacing may be sufficient. For high-speed, RF, or high-EMI areas, the spacing may need to be reduced. Common engineering reference values include: General PCBs: approximately 50–100 mil High-speed/RF areas: approximately 30–50 mil Areas with stringent shielding requirements: further spacing reduction based on simulation or actual EMI testing Do not mechanically apply a fixed value. The final via spacing should be determined based on the actual frequency and structure. 2. Via Location Edge grounding vias should maintain an appropriate clearance from the PCB outline. Sufficient clearance should be provided according to the PCB manufacturer's fabrication capability to prevent damage to the vias during routing, milling, V-cut, or other board-edge processing. At the same time: Distribute the vias evenly along the board edge whenever possible. Avoid large gaps in the via fence. Increase via density around RF, high-speed signal, and connector areas when necessary. Connect the grounding vias to the appropriate reference ground plane rather than only to the top-layer copper. It is important to note that not every ground plane needs to be connected through the same via. The exact connection method should be determined based on the PCB stackup and return-current path. 3. Start With Continuous Ground Copper Many designers add a row of vias but overlook the ground copper between them. This alone cannot create a complete PCB ground via fence. A continuous ground copper area should be provided around the PCB edge according to the board structure, with grounding vias connecting it to the internal reference ground plane. The vias provide vertical connections, while continuous ground copper provides horizontal connections. Together, they form a more complete grounding boundary. High-speed signal traces, slots, or other structures should not arbitrarily cut through this grounding boundary. 4. Increase Via Density in Critical Areas The entire PCB does not necessarily need the same via spacing. The following areas may require additional stitching vias: Board-edge connectors and interfaces: Connectors are important paths through which external signals enter the PCB. Proper grounding vias can improve the return path around the interface and reduce edge coupling. Shielding-can areas: Dense grounding vias around the shielding-can solder pad can create a more continuous high-frequency grounding path. RF and high-speed clock areas: For areas that are particularly sensitive to EMI or crosstalk, reducing the via spacing can strengthen local shielding. Conclusion Proper stitching vias are an important part of high-speed PCB layout and PCB design .Their core function is to improve high-frequency return paths around the PCB edge and reduce electromagnetic coupling and EMI leakage through the combination of stitching vias and continuous reference-ground structures. For high-speed, RF, and EMI-sensitive PCBs, proper PCB via stitching and PCB edge shielding are particularly important. But remember: more vias are not always better, and not every PCB needs a dense row of grounding vias. Via spacing, edge clearance, reference planes, and local shielding structures should all be determined based on the actual signal frequency, rise time, and PCB stackup. Sheets generally include fr-4, cem-3, etc., and board thickness varies from 0.2mm to 5.0mm, and copper thickness varies from 0.5oz to 3oz. All of these have resulted in huge price differences on the sheet material; in solder mask inks, there are also certain price differences between ordinary thermoset oils and photosensitive green oils, and thus the diversity of materials has caused price diversity. The different production processes used by PCBs result in different production processes with different prices that will result in different costs. Such as gold-plated plates and sprayed tin plates, the production of the shape of the milling (milling) plate and beer (red) plate, the use of silk screen lines and dry film lines will have different costs, resulting in a variety of prices. The diversity of prices caused by the difficulty of the PCB itself Even if the material is the same, the process is the same, but the difficulty of the PCB itself will result in different costs. For example, if there are 1000 holes on both boards, the hole diameter of one board is more than 0.6mm and the hole diameter of the other board is less than 0.6mm, different drilling costs will be formed; if the two boards are the same, the linewidth is different. Differently, one type is larger than 0.2mm and one type is smaller than 0.2mm, which also causes different production costs, because the scrap rate of difficult plates is high, the inevitable cost is increased, and the price diversity is thus caused. Different customer requirements will also cause different prices The level of customer demand will directly affect the plate production rate, such as a board by ipc-a-600e, class1 requirements have a 98% pass rate, but according to class3 requirements may be only 90% The passing rate, resulting in different costs for the mill, eventually led to a change in the price of the product. The diversity of prices caused by different PCB manufacturers even if the same product, but because of different manufacturers of technology and equipment, different levels of technology, will also form a different cost, nowadays many manufacturers like to produce tin spray plate, because the process is simple, low cost, but Some manufacturers also produce gold-plated plates, resulting in higher scrap rates and higher costs. Therefore, they prefer to produce tin-spray plates, so their prices for tin-spray plates are lower than those for gold-plated plates. The price difference caused by different payment methods At present, PCB manufacturers generally adjust PCB prices according to different payment methods, ranging from 5% to 10%, which also results in price differences. Diversification of prices caused by regional differences At present, from the geographical point of view, prices have been increasing from south to north. There are certain differences in prices in different regions, and thus different regions have also caused price diversity. Its 170 × 170 mm PCB contains 225 individually addressable Worldsemi WS2812B-2427-V6 LEDs at 10 mm spacing. A serpentine data chain allows an external microcontroller to control the entire panel through one signal output. The board uses a three-wire DATA, GND and regulated 5 V interface, with supply capacitors, an input pulldown and an output test pad for troubleshooting. Intended applications include pixel art, animated patterns, ambient lighting and a clock Engineer 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. A serpentine data chain allows an external microcontroller to control the entire panel through one signal output. The board uses a three-wire DATA, GND and regulated 5 V interface, with supply capacitors, an input pulldown and an output test pad for troubleshooting. Intended applications include pixel art, animated patterns, ambient lighting and a clock Engineer 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design. Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. Engineer 15x15 Adressible RGB LED Panel [PCB Assembly] This project is a custom 15 × 15 RGB LED panel designed as the display core of a pixel-art mood lamp. Its 170 × 170 mm PCB contains 225 individually addressable Worldsemi WS2812B-2427-V6 LEDs at 10 mm spacing. A serpentine data chain allows an external microcontroller to control the entire panel through one signal output. The board uses a three-wire DATA, GND and regulated 5 V interface, with supply capacitors, an input pulldown and an output test pad for troubleshooting. Intended applications include pixel art, animated patterns, ambient lighting and a clock Engineer 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design. Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. Each PCB has a unique function for a particular product. Therefore, producing a PCB is a complex process of many steps. This overview covers the most important steps when producing a multilayer PCB. When you order PCBs from the PCBWay, you are buying quality that pays for itself over time. This is guaranteed through a product specification and quality control that is far more stringent than other suppliers, and ensures that the product delivers what it promises. In the production flow below you can see where the PCBWay process is unique or goes beyond the IPC standard. Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. Artwork Master – The photographic image of the PCB pattern on film used to produce the circuit board, usually on a 1:1 scale.In general, there are three types of Artwork Master:(1) Conductive Pattern (2) solder mask (3) Silkscreen Put away 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. Hide Details 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. Hide Details 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design. Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. Hide Details 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. Hide Details 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. Hide Details 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill Hide Details 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. Hide Details 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. Hide Details 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. Hide Details 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. Hide Details 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. Hide Details 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. Hide Details 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. Hide Details 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. Hide Details 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. Hide Details 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. Hide Details 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. BGAs (Ball Grid Arrays) are a type of IC package where the pins are placed in the form of solder balls. Compared to traditional packaging technologies such as DIP (Dual In-line Package) or QFP (Quad Flat Package), BGA employs a higher-density pin layout. With technological advancements, there is an increasing demand in PCB design for complex and small-sized chips. These chips enable higher integration and functionality within smaller spaces. Hence, there is a need for a packaging method that can accommodate these chips with higher I/O density while maintaining cost-effectiveness. BGA (Ball Grid Array) is precisely such a packaging method that meets these requirements. What is BGA Assembly? BGA assembly refers to the process of mounting a Ball Grid Array (BGA) onto a PCB using the reflow soldering technique. BGA is a surface-mounted component that utilizes an array of solder balls for electrical interconnection. As the circuit board passes through a solder reflow oven, these solder balls melt, forming electrical connections. Steps of BGA Assembly The BGA assembly process typically involves the following steps: PCB Preparation: The PCB is prepared by applying solder paste to the pads where the BGA will be mounted. The solder paste is a mixture of solder alloy particles and flux, which helps with the soldering process. Placement of BGAs: The BGAs, which consist of the integrated circuit chip with solder balls on the bottom, are placed onto the prepared PCB. This is typically done using automated pick-and-place machines or other assembly equipment. Reflow Soldering: The assembled PCB with the placed BGAs is then passed through a reflow oven. The reflow oven heats the PCB to a specific temperature that melts the solder paste, causing the solder balls of the BGAs to reflow and establish electrical connections with the PCB pads. Cooling and Inspection: After the solder reflow process, the PCB is cooled down to solidify the solder joints. It is then inspected for any defects, such as misalignment, shorts, or open connections. Automated optical inspection (AOI) or X-ray inspection may be used for this purpose. Secondary Processes: Depending on the specific requirements, additional processes such as cleaning, testing, and conformal coating may be performed after BGA assembly to ensure the reliability and quality of the finished product. Advantages of BGA Assembly Small footprint BGA packaging consists of the chip, interconnects, a thin substrate, and an encapsulation cover. There are few exposed components and the package has a minimal number of pins. The overall height of the chip on the PCB can be as low as 1.2 millimeters. Robustness BGA packaging is highly robust. Unlike QFP with a 20mil pitch, BGA does not have pins that can bend or break. Generally, BGA removal requires the use of a BGA rework station at high temperatures. Lower parasitic inductance and capacitance With short pins and low assembly height, BGA packaging exhibits low parasitic inductance and capacitance, resulting in excellent electrical performance. Increased storage space Compared to other packaging types, BGA packaging has only one-third of the volume and approximately 1.2 times the chip area. Memory and operational products using BGA packaging can achieve more than a 2.1-fold increase in storage capacity and operational speed. High stability Due to the direct extension of pins from the center of the chip in BGA packaging, the transmission paths for various signals are effectively shortened, reducing signal attenuation and improving response speed and anti-interference capabilities. This enhances the stability of the product. Good heat dissipation BGA offers excellent heat dissipation performance, with the chip temperature approaching the ambient temperature during operation. Convenient for rework The pins of BGA packaging are neatly arranged on the bottom, making it easy to locate damaged areas for removal. This facilitates the rework of BGA chips. Avoidance of wiring chaos BGA packaging allows for placing many power and ground pins in the center, with I/O pins positioned on the periphery. Pre-routing can be done on the BGA substrate, avoiding chaotic wiring of I/O pins. PCBWay BGA Assembly Capabilities PCBWay is a globally renowned manufacturer for PCB fabrication and PCB assembly. BGAs (Ball Grid Arrays) are a type of IC package where the pins are placed in the form of solder balls. Compared to traditional packaging technologies such as DIP (Dual In-line Package) or QFP (Quad Flat Package), BGA employs a higher-density pin layout. With technological advancements, there is an increasing demand in PCB design for complex and small-sized chips. These chips enable higher integration and functionality within smaller spaces. Hence, there is a need for a packaging method that can accommodate these chips with higher I/O density while maintaining cost-effectiveness. BGA (Ball Grid Array) is precisely such a packaging method that meets these requirements. What is BGA Assembly? BGA assembly refers to the process of mounting a Ball Grid Array (BGA) onto a PCB using the reflow soldering technique. BGA is a surface-mounted component that utilizes an array of solder balls for electrical interconnection. As the circuit board passes through a solder reflow oven, these solder balls melt, forming electrical connections. Steps of BGA Assembly The BGA assembly process typically involves the following steps: PCB Preparation: The PCB is prepared by applying solder paste to the pads where the BGA will be mounted. The solder paste is a mixture of solder alloy particles and flux, which helps with the soldering process. Placement of BGAs: The BGAs, which consist of the integrated circuit chip with solder balls on the bottom, are placed onto the prepared PCB. This is typically done using automated pick-and-place machines or other assembly equipment. Reflow Soldering: The assembled PCB with the placed BGAs is then passed through a reflow oven. The reflow oven heats the PCB to a specific temperature that melts the solder paste, causing the solder balls of the BGAs to reflow and establish electrical connections with the PCB pads. Cooling and Inspection: After the solder reflow process, the PCB is cooled down to solidify the solder joints. It is then inspected for any defects, such as misalignment, shorts, or open connections. Automated optical inspection (AOI) or X-ray inspection may be used for this purpose. Secondary Processes: Depending on the specific requirements, additional processes such as cleaning, testing, and conformal coating may be performed after BGA assembly to ensure the reliability and quality of the finished product. Advantages of BGA Assembly Small footprint BGA packaging consists of the chip, interconnects, a thin substrate, and an encapsulation cover. There are few exposed components and the package has a minimal number of pins. The overall height of the chip on the PCB can be as low as 1.2 millimeters. Robustness BGA packaging is highly robust. Unlike QFP with a 20mil pitch, BGA does not have pins that can bend or break. Generally, BGA removal requires the use of a BGA rework station at high temperatures. Lower parasitic inductance and capacitance With short pins and low assembly height, BGA packaging exhibits low parasitic inductance and capacitance, resulting in excellent electrical performance. Increased storage space Compared to other packaging types, BGA packaging has only one-third of the volume and approximately 1.2 times the chip area. Memory and operational products using BGA packaging can achieve more than a 2.1-fold increase in storage capacity and operational speed. High stability Due to the direct extension of pins from the center of the chip in BGA packaging, the transmission paths for various signals are effectively shortened, reducing signal attenuation and improving response speed and anti-interference capabilities. This enhances the stability of the product. Good heat dissipation BGA offers excellent heat dissipation performance, with the chip temperature approaching the ambient temperature during operation. Convenient for rework The pins of BGA packaging are neatly arranged on the bottom, making it easy to locate damaged areas for removal. This facilitates the rework of BGA chips. Avoidance of wiring chaos BGA packaging allows for placing many power and ground pins in the center, with I/O pins positioned on the periphery. Pre-routing can be done on the BGA substrate, avoiding chaotic wiring of I/O pins. PCBWay BGA Assembly Capabilities PCBWay is a globally renowned manufacturer for PCB fabrication and PCB assembly. BGA assembly service is one of the many service types we offer. PCBWay can provide you with high-quality and cost-effective BGA assembly for your PCBs. The minimum pitch for BGA assembly that we can accommodate is 0.25mm 0.3mm . SMT, which stands for Surface Mount Technology, is a method of directly mounting electronic components onto the surface of a PCB. This method is commonly used for installing Surface Mount Devices (SMDs), which have smaller pins or are pinless in structure. Compared to traditional through-hole technology, SMT provides higher levels of automated manufacturing capabilities, reduces costs, and improves quality. Additionally, SMT allows for the installation of more components on a limited PCB board area. Through-hole technology is typically used for components such as large transformers and high-power heat-dissipating semiconductors that are not suitable for surface mounting. SMT components have smaller leads or no leads at all, and common structures include short pins or leads, flat contacts, and Ball Grid Arrays (BGAs). PCBWay SMT Assembly Capability Overview We have the capabilities to assemble SMT prototype PCBs in small production runs with manual and/or automated SMT production processes, including single- or double-sided component insertions. Get a quote Rapid Prototyping 3D Printing Digital Light Processing (DLP) Overview Processes Materials Finishes Industries Reviews Resources Quote Now! Overview:What Is a DLP 3D Printer? How Do DLP 3D Printers Work? Digital Light Processing is a 3d printing process where a projector is used to cure photopolymer resin. Very similar to SLA where the only difference is that instead of a UV laser to cure the photopolymer resin, a safelight (light bulb) is used. Objects are created the same as SLA with the object being either pulled out of the resin which creates space for the uncured resin at the bottom of the container and to form the next layer of the object or down into the tank with the next layer being cured on the top. A diagram illustrated the DLP setup. Source: DruckWege.de Objects that are printed with Digital Light Processing have less visible layers versus other processes such as FDM/FFF. Compared with SLA, DLP can have faster build speeds due to a single layer being created in one singular digital image whereas with SLA, the UV laser has to scan the vat with a single point (trace out the object layer). Also, the same photopolymer resins that can be used with SLA, can be used for DLP 3D Printing. Objects printed with this process have the same strengths and weaknesses. Similar to SLA, DLP is commonly used to generate highly detailed artwork, non-functional prototypes, and can be used to make molds in investment casting applications. Main DLP 3D Printing Technologies Digital Light Processing provides excellent capabilities for 3D printing / Additive Manufacturing processes with an eye on efficiency. DLP is your go-to method when opting for a quick printing process without compromising on the quality of intricate parts. Just like their SLA counterparts, desktop DLP 3D printers are built around a resin tank with transparent bottom and a build platform that descends into a resin tank to create parts upside down, layer by layer. The difference is the light source. DLP 3D printers use a digital projector screen to flash an image of a layer across the entire platform, curing all points simultaneously.Now that you know how SLA works, it’s time to take a closer look at DLP. DLP is a “sister technology” to SLA as the only big difference is the light source used to cure the resin. As we just mentioned, SLA printers use lasers combined with galvanometers to cure resin. With a DLP 3D printer, the light source is a specially developed digital light projector screen. Thanks to this screen, DLP is generally considered to be faster than SLA, and here’s why: With SLA, the laser has to individually cure the resin in a “point to point” technique. On the other hand, a DLP projector screen flashes an image of a layer all at once! Thus all points of a layer can be cured simultaneously. In this way, the print speed is increased in comparison to SLA since it takes less time to cure a single layer. Since the DLP is a digital technology, the 2D image that is projected is composed of pixels. When translated into three dimensions, they become voxels. Get a quote Rapid Prototyping 3D Printing Digital Light Processing (DLP) Overview Processes Materials Finishes Industries Reviews Resources Quote Now! Overview:What Is a DLP 3D Printer? How Do DLP 3D Printers Work? Digital Light Processing is a 3d printing process where a projector is used to cure photopolymer resin. Very similar to SLA where the only difference is that instead of a UV laser to cure the photopolymer resin, a safelight (light bulb) is used. Objects are created the same as SLA with the object being either pulled out of the resin which creates space for the uncured resin at the bottom of the container and to form the next layer of the object or down into the tank with the next layer being cured on the top. A diagram illustrated the DLP setup. Source: DruckWege.de Objects that are printed with Digital Light Processing have less visible layers versus other processes such as FDM/FFF. Compared with SLA, DLP can have faster build speeds due to a single layer being created in one singular digital image whereas with SLA, the UV laser has to scan the vat with a single point (trace out the object layer). Also, the same photopolymer resins that can be used with SLA, can be used for DLP 3D Printing. Objects printed with this process have the same strengths and weaknesses. Similar to SLA, DLP is commonly used to generate highly detailed artwork, non-functional prototypes, and can be used to make molds in investment casting applications. Main DLP 3D Printing Technologies Digital Light Processing provides excellent capabilities for 3D printing / Additive Manufacturing processes with an eye on efficiency. DLP is your go-to method when opting for a quick printing process without compromising on the quality of intricate parts. Just like their SLA counterparts, desktop DLP 3D printers are built around a resin tank with transparent bottom and a build platform that descends into a resin tank to create parts upside down, layer by layer. The difference is the light source. DLP 3D printers use a digital projector screen to flash an image of a layer across the entire platform, curing all points simultaneously.Now that you know how SLA works, it’s time to take a closer look at DLP. DLP is a “sister technology” to SLA as the only big difference is the light source used to cure the resin. As we just mentioned, SLA printers use lasers combined with galvanometers to cure resin. With a DLP 3D printer, the light source is a specially developed digital light projector screen. Thanks to this screen, DLP is generally considered to be faster than SLA, and here’s why: With SLA, the laser has to individually cure the resin in a “point to point” technique. On the other hand, a DLP projector screen flashes an image of a layer all at once! Thus all points of a layer can be cured simultaneously. In this way, the print speed is increased in comparison to SLA since it takes less time to cure a single layer. Since the DLP is a digital technology, the 2D image that is projected is composed of pixels. When translated into three dimensions, they become voxels.
